name: Mog-offs (AI face battles)

lead: A mog-off is a face-versus-face contest in which two people join a video chat and facial-rating software compares them and declares a winner. 'Mogging' in looksmaxxing slang means outshining someone in looks.
Participants use the results as feedback and to compare themselves before and after changes such as grooming or fitness.

paras: Two people go on camera while the software scores each face; the higher score wins the round.

Results come from whichever software is used and depend on the photo and the model. Appearance-rating apps have drawn commentary from mental-health and online-safety writers about effects on young users, and random video chat formats raise moderation and privacy questions.

angle.text: The format gives users a quick comparative score they can track after appearance changes.

lead: A mog-off is a one-on-one contest in which AI software rates two faces and names a winner, borrowing from 'mogging', the community term for one person looking better than another.[1] People use it as a game and as quick comparative feedback on how their face scores, including before and after changes in grooming, skin or fitness.[2][3]

The best-known version is Omoggle, a play on the defunct Omegle, which places two people side by side on video and estimates which face is closer to an idealised beauty standard. It became a fad among Twitch streamers in 2026 after Twitch amended its rule on randomised video chat services.[2] Other tools run the comparison on two uploaded photos and return per-person scores, a verdict and a radar chart of facial dimensions.[3]
No published study has evaluated these tools. Coverage by child-safety and mental-health commentators discusses their effect on young users.[4]

paras: The winner is called the 'Mogger' and the loser 'Mogged'. Scores are commonly given on the PSL scale, the looksmaxxing rating that runs from roughly 0 to 8.[1][3]

One photo-based comparison tool describes eight scored dimensions weighted into an overall PSL number: symmetry, harmony, proportions, skin quality, facial structure, averageness, sexual dimorphism and memorable features. Its bands label 3.5 to 5.4 as average and 7.0 to 8.0 as elite, and its operator states that results depend on the photo and the model.[3]
Users export share cards and post them in group chats or timelines, and use the radar view to see which dimensions drove a result.[3]

Streamers helped popularise Omoggle, and its leaderboard lists thousands of players. Twitch had barred it under the guideline on randomised video chat services, then amended the guideline so streamers could use it.[2]

Commentators writing on looksmaxxing say that appearance-focused content can intersect with body dysmorphic disorder and eating disorders, particularly among teen boys and young men.[4] Randomised video chat formats have historically raised moderation issues, and facial scans raise privacy questions, according to news coverage of the app.

lore.intro: Mog-offs sit within the wider mogging and PSL vocabulary of looksmaxxing.[1]

claims.claim: AI scores show how one's face ranks against others

timeline.event: Omoggle spreads on Twitch after the platform amends its rule on randomised video chat services.[2]
